newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel leaves options open as budget gap grows.
newsitem.headline: Waigel leaves options open as budget gap grows.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, under pressure to plug a widening budget gap, said on Thursday he would step up privatisations, tap Bundesbank reserves and declined to rule out tax increases.

Finding it increasingly difficult to hold the budget deficit down far enough to qualify for Europe's planned single currency, Waigel said he was not ruling out any measure after it became clear that tax revenues in 1997 and 1998 would come in well below target.

As Waigel was set to outline the situation to a meeting of parliament deputies from the government coalition in the evening, he said Bonn planned to take the controversial step of drawing on the Bundesbank's gold and currency reserves.

While he insisted Germany would not sell "an ounce of gold," he said the government would revalue the gold from low book rates to current market prices, which analysts said could raise over 40 billion marks ($23.6 billion) to pay off old debt.
But Waigel made clear he had no quick fix to offer.
"This is not a problem that can be solved in a day," he said. "We will step up privatisations, enforce strict spending cuts, and measures for 1998 will be decided in July."
Waigel reiterated his belief that Germany was still on track to qualify for European economic and monetary union (EMU) -- with or without special measures to rein in the budget deficit.
"We will achieve the 3.0 percent deficit criterion," he said. "It might be possible without additional measures but that would not be certain."

A panel of government and private tax experts presented the latest tax estimate that predicted 1997 revenues would be around 18 billion marks below previous forecasts. Federal tax receipts alone would come in 9.1 billion marks below forecasts.
Germany's 1997 budget sees a deficit of 53.3 billion marks. Economists expect Waigel to present a supplementary budget to account for this gap in revenue.

The tax shortfall, which seriously threatens Germany's EMU bid, has largely been brought about by record unemployment, which Waigel said would average 4.3 million this year and could require additional spending of up to 20 billion marks.
But there are other factors affecting tax revenues such as weak consumer spending and the use of tax loopholes that many Germans have perfected.
"The use of tax write-offs played a much larger role than ever before. This has convinced me more than ever that structural changes are needed," Waigel said.
Waigel gave few indications of how he planned to offset the declining revenues. "Nothing can be ruled out," he said.
The government is widely expected to increase petrol taxes, a move that would increase revenues but have little impact on inflation and therefore be likely to help Germany's EMU bid.
But any tax hike is likely to face fierce opposition from the liberal Free Democrats (FDP), Chancellor Helmut Kohl's junior coalition partner.
"We do not want any tax increases because we want a policy of tax cuts to help create jobs," said FDP general secretary Guido Westerwelle.
Waigel said the government was still considering a spending freeze, but he made clear he did not believe this would have much of an impact on the budget.
He also suggested there could be changes to corporate tax rules that would make it more difficult for companies to carry forward losses from previous years and thereby reduce current tax burdens.

Hoping to counter the effects of capital flight, which robs Germany of huge tax revenues each year as Germans invest in tax havens, Waigel called for a "code of conduct" with Germany's European neighbours.

The government is also giving serious consideration to selling more of its shares in phone monopoly Deutsche Telekom AG. Bonn still holds a stake of 74 percent, which is currently worth some 80 billion marks.

Selling just 10 percent of the government's over two billion shares in Deutsche Telekom at a discount in private placements to institutional investors could raise between seven and eight billion marks this year.
